findings.claim: `processedSet` is declared inside the per-method loop, so it is re-created on every iteration and can never carry state between handler sets — it is exactly equivalent to the old `!i` test, only with an extra object allocation per iteration (including when `handlerSet` is undefined, on a hot routing path).
findings.rationale: The map is keyed by `handlerSet.score`, which only makes sense if the intent was to remember "this score was already processed" across the outer `for (let i = 0; i < node.#methods.length; i++)` loop. As written the declaration sits inside that loop and is reset each time, so the keying is dead weight. Either the declaration belongs outside the loop (in which case this is a real logic bug — the intended dedup never happens) or the whole map should be dropped in favour of `!i`. Also note the allocation now happens before the `handlerSet !== undefined` check, so it is paid even for methods with no matching handler, which works against the apparent perf goal of this change. Fairly confident this is at minimum wasted work, and likely an intent bug.

findings.claim: Keying the processed flag on `handlerSet.score` rather than on the key index is unsafe if this map is ever hoisted out of the loop: scores are not guaranteed unique across different handler sets.
findings.rationale: `score` is a route-ordering value, and two distinct handler sets matched by the same node can plausibly share a score. If `processedSet` is later moved outside the loop (which is the only way it has any effect), a collision would silently cause the second handler set's first possible key to ignore the incoming `params` and fall back to `nodeParams`, producing wrong path parameters. Flagging as a latent correctness hazard rather than a current bug.

findings.claim: Skipping the key loop when both `nodeParams` and `params` are the shared `emptyParams` sentinel changes observable behavior: previously each `possibleKeys[key]` was explicitly assigned (possibly `undefined`), so the key existed on `handlerSet.params`; now those keys are absent entirely.
findings.rationale: `Object.create(null)` plus no assignments means `'id' in handlerSet.params` is false and `Object.keys(handlerSet.params)` is empty, whereas before both would report the key. Any downstream code that enumerates params or uses `in`/`hasOwnProperty` (e.g. `c.req.param()` returning the full record) would see a different shape. Value-level reads (`params[key]`) still yield `undefined`, so this is only a problem for enumeration/existence checks — but it is a genuine behavior change for existing callers. Medium confidence that something downstream cares.

findings.claim: The guard relies on reference identity with `emptyParams`; any caller that passes a freshly-created empty object, or a `nodeParams` that is empty but not the sentinel, takes the slow path and (more importantly) produces a different `handlerSet.params` shape than the sentinel path.
findings.rationale: Two logically identical inputs (empty params) now yield different results depending on whether the caller happened to reuse the shared sentinel: sentinel → keys absent, other empty object → keys present with `undefined`. That inconsistency is easy to trip over as the codebase evolves. Also note `params` is null-checked (`params && params !== emptyParams`) but `nodeParams` is dereferenced unguarded at line 79 — fine if `nodeParams` is non-optional, but worth confirming against the signature.

findings.claim: `params?.[key] &&` is a truthiness test, so an empty-string path parameter value in `params` is treated as absent and falls through to `nodeParams[key] ?? params?.[key]`.
findings.rationale: Pre-existing behavior that this change preserves rather than introduces, but since the line is being rewritten it is worth deciding deliberately: the correct check for "the incoming params supplied this key" is `params?.[key] !== undefined`. Low impact if empty-string captures are impossible in this matcher, which I could not verify from the hunk alone.
